sections.title: How does the Meat footprint calculator work?
sections.html:
The Meat footprint calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports footprint areas in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the chicken/poultry (My actual meat consumption), the pork (My actual meat consumption), the lamb (My actual meat consumption) and the fish (My actual meat consumption).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Meat footprint calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Give me my meat footprint for a=5 × landuse ÷ (1631 × beef − 1631 × beef × I want to know + 61 × chicken ÷ poultry − 61 × chicken ÷ poultry × I want to know + 42 × fish − 42 × fish × I want to know + 1849 × lamb − 1849 × lamb × I want to know + 87 × pork − 87 × pork × I want to know)
Water pollution=(1 ÷ 10) × give me my meat footprint for a... × (3014 × beef − 3014 × beef × I want to know + 487 × chicken ÷ poultry − 487 × chicken ÷ poultry × I want to know + 2351 × fish − 2351 × fish × I want to know + 971 × lamb − 971 × lamb × I want to know + 764 × pork − 764 × pork × I want to know)
Give me my meat footprint for a=10 × air pollution ÷ (3188 × beef − 3188 × beef × I want to know + 1024 × chicken ÷ poultry − 1024 × chicken ÷ poultry × I want to know + 659 × fish − 659 × fish × I want to know + 1390 × lamb − 1390 × lamb × I want to know + 1427 × pork − 1427 × pork × I want to know)
Protein from meat=(1 ÷ 5) × beef + (7 ÷ 40) × chicken ÷ poultry + (23 ÷ 100) × fish + (1 ÷ 5) × lamb + (4 ÷ 25) × pork
Chicken/poultry=(200 ÷ 17) × chicken ÷ poultry
Beef=(200 ÷ 17) × beef

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Meat footprint calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Putting a headline figure into context
  • Sizing an environmental impact in familiar units
  • Comparing two options on the same basis
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the chicken/poultry and the pork — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Meat footprint calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns footprint areas, derived from the chicken/poultry and the pork. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Meat footprint calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the chicken/poultry and the pork, which is 17 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter chicken/poultry (My actual meat consumption) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Chicken/poultry (My actual meat consumption) opens in weeks and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Beef = 0 g. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Meat footprint calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
